summary.text: Direct evaluation gives \(a(5)=171\) and \(a(6)=X=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761\), with \(X\equiv3\pmod{18}\). Since \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{171}\), it follows that \(2^X+1\equiv2^3+1\equiv9\not\equiv0\pmod{171}\), so the required divisibility fails at \(n=7\).

full_proof.text:
Let the sequence be defined by
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}\quad(n\geq 3).
\]
We will compute the terms through \(a(6)\), show that all divisions up to that point are exact, and then show that the division defining \(a(7)\) is not exact.

The first few terms are immediate:
\[
a(3)=\frac{2^{a(2)}+1}{a(1)}=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,
\]
\[
a(4)=\frac{2^{a(3)}+1}{a(2)}=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,
\]
and
\[
a(5)=\frac{2^{a(4)}+1}{a(3)}=\frac{2^9+1}{3}
     =\frac{512+1}{3}=171.
\]
Thus the next term is
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
This quotient is an integer. For instance, \(2^6\equiv1\pmod 9\), and since \(171=6\cdot28+3\),
\[
2^{171}\equiv 2^3\equiv8\equiv-1\pmod9.
\]
Hence \(9\mid 2^{171}+1\).

Set
\[
X=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761.
\]
A direct exponentiation and multiplication give
\[
2^{171}=2993155353253689176481146537402947624255349848014848
\]
and
\[
9X=2993155353253689176481146537402947624255349848014849
   =2^{171}+1.
\]
Consequently
\[
a(6)=X.
\]
Thus all of \(a(1),\ldots,a(6)\) are integers, and the division whose exactness must next be tested is
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{a(5)}=\frac{2^X+1}{171}.
\]
It remains to show that \(171\) does not divide \(2^X+1\).

First note that \(X\) has the following division by \(18\):
\[
X=18q+3,
\]
where
\[
q=18476267612677093681982386033351528544786110172931.
\]
Next, compute
\[
2^{18}=262144=171\cdot1533+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{171}.
\]
Using \(X=18q+3\), we now reduce the numerator defining \(a(7)\) modulo \(171\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^X+1
  &=2^{18q+3}+1\\
  &=(2^{18})^q2^3+1\\
  &\equiv 1^q\cdot8+1\pmod{171}\\
  &\equiv9\pmod{171}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The residue \(9\) is nonzero modulo \(171\), since \(0<9<171\). Hence
\[
171\nmid 2^X+1.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^X+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer. Therefore the assertion that every term of the sequence is an integer is false; the first failure exhibited here occurs at the seventh term.
